lead: The 8051 has four 8-bit parallel ports, P0 to P3. Each port is a latch plus an output driver, and that pair explains every rule of port programming: to use a pin as an input you first write 1 to it, so the driver stops holding the pin low and a weak internal pull-up can raise it. Some instructions then read the pin, others read the latch. LEDs, switches, keypads, relays and LCD panels all connect through these ports, which makes them the most-used pins on the chip.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for the port SFR addresses, bit addressing and the pin functions of P3.

blocks.text: The four port registers are special function registers at fixed direct addresses: P0 at 80H, P1 at 90H, P2 at A0H and P3 at B0H. All four are bit addressable, so P1.3 means bit 3 of P1, bit address 93H. Writing a byte to P1 writes its latch; the latch output drives the pin through an output transistor.

P0 is open drain. Its driver can pull a pin to 0 V but has no pull-up of its own, so it cannot pull a pin high. Put an external resistor from the pin to +5 V (10 kΩ is a common choice) or the pin floats when its latch holds 1. P0 also becomes the multiplexed address/data bus AD0–AD7 when external memory is used.

P1, P2 and P3 are quasi-bidirectional. Each pin has a weak internal pull-up. Writing 1 to the latch switches the strong driver off, and the weak pull-up holds the pin near +5 V; an external circuit that pulls the pin low wins, because the pull-up supplies only tens of microamps. Writing 0 switches the strong driver on and forces the pin to 0 V.

A pin sinks more current than it sources: the classic part lists about 1.6 mA sink for P1–P3 and 3.2 mA for P0, but only a small source current. So an LED is wired with its anode to +5 V through a resistor and its cathode to the pin: pin low means LED on.
P2 supplies A8–A15 in expanded memory systems. P3 pins carry RXD, TXD, INT0, INT1, T0, T1, WR and RD, so check those chapters before using P3 as plain I/O (see 4.3, 4.4, 4.5).

If the latch holds 0, the driver holds the pin at 0 V. A switch to ground then changes nothing, and the CPU always reads 0. Writing 1 turns the driver off, so a switch, keypad or sensor output can decide the pin level. The standard line before reading a port is MOV P1,#0FFH.

Two kinds of instruction touch a port. Read-pin instructions look at the outside world. Read-modify-write instructions (RMW) read the latch, change it, and write it back, so an external load that drags the pin slowly cannot be misread as the value the software intended.

Reads

INC P1 ; DEC P1 ; CPL P1.0

blocks.text: The table is the examinable core: when the port is the destination of a logical or bit instruction, the latch value is used, not the voltage on the pin.
Blink an LED on P1.0 in assembly. CPL P1.0 is read-modify-write, which is safe here because the pin is an output.

blocks.code:
ORG 0000H
        MOV P1,#00H          ; every P1 pin driven low
AGAIN:  CPL P1.0             ; toggle the LED pin
        ACALL DELAY
        SJMP AGAIN
DELAY:  MOV R7,#200
D1:     MOV R6,#250
D2:     DJNZ R6,D2
        DJNZ R7,D1
        RET
        END

blocks.text: The delay is about 200 × 250 × 2 = 100000 machine cycles, roughly 0.1 s with a 12 MHz crystal (1 µs per machine cycle).
Copy a switch on P1.1 to the LED on P1.0. MOV C,P1.1 reads the pin; MOV P1.0,C writes the latch bit.

blocks.code:
MOV P1,#0FFH         ; release all pins: P1.1 can be an input
READ:   MOV C,P1.1           ; read the switch pin
        MOV P1.0,C           ; drive the LED pin
        SJMP READ

blocks.text: The same job in C for Keil-style 8051 compilers:

Masking changes some bits and keeps the rest: P1 = (P1 & 0xF0) | 0x05; keeps P1.4–P1.7 and sets P1.0 and P1.2. The compiler reads P1 with MOV A,P1, which reads the pin, unlike the 8051's own RMW instruction. Any pin used as an input must already have its latch at 1, or the mask writes 0 back to it.

figure.caption: Writing 1 releases the pin, the switch pulls it to ground, and MOV A,P1 reports 0 while the latch still holds 1. Every read-modify-write instruction follows the dashed path.

spec.title: Reading a port pin
spec.aria: Flow of reading an 8051 port pin: write 1 to the latch, let a switch pull the pin low, read the pin, while the latch stays high for read-modify-write instructions.

examples.question: Port 1 is written 0FFH. An external switch from P1.0 to ground is closed and holds that pin low. The program then runs MOV A,P1 / ANL P1,#0FH / MOV A,P1. Give A after the first read, the P1 latch after ANL, and A after the second read. (Hex and decimal.)
steps: Initial latch P1 = 1111 1111 = FFH. The switch holds pin P1.0 at 0; pins P1.1–P1.7 have latch 1 and nothing pulling them, so the weak pull-up makes them 1.
MOV A,P1 reads the pin: 1111 1110 = FEH = 254. So A = 254.
ANL P1,#0FH is read-modify-write. It reads the latch (FFH), not the pin (FEH): FFH AND 0FH = 0FH = 15. The latch becomes 15, so P1.4–P1.7 latch bits are 0 and those pins are driven low.
ANL P1,#0FH does not touch A, so A is still 254.
Second MOV A,P1 reads the pin. P1.7–P1.4 are driven low = 0000. P1.3–P1.1 have latch 1 and are released = 111. P1.0 is still held by the switch = 0. Pin byte = 0000 1110 = 0EH = 14. So A = 14.
examples.answer: A = FEH (254) after the first read, the P1 latch becomes 0FH (15) after the ANL, and A = 0EH (14) after the second read.
examples.check:
latch = 0xFF
switch = 0x01          # bits an external switch holds at 0

def read_pin(latch, switch):
    return latch & ~switch & 0xFF   # latch 0 drives the pin low; switch overrides 1 to 0

A = read_pin(latch, switch)
print(A)                # 254 = FEH
latch = latch & 0x0F    # ANL P1,#0FH reads the latch
print(latch)            # 15 = 0FH
A = read_pin(latch, switch)
print(A)                # 14 = 0EH

traps: Writing 0 to a pin and then expecting an external switch to change it. The driver holds the pin low, so the CPU always reads 0. Write 1 first.
Mixing up MOV A,P1 (reads the pin) with ANL P1,#data (reads the latch). Examiners love giving a latch value, a switch position and two reads, then asking for both A and P1.
Forgetting that P0 is open drain. Without external pull-up resistors P0 cannot produce a logic 1, so an LED or gate on P0 with no resistor never goes high.
Believing that writing 1 to P1, P2 or P3 drives the pin strongly high. It only releases the pin to a weak pull-up; the pin can still be pulled low, and it cannot source an LED.
Reading a whole port in C (P1 = P1 | 0x0F) reads the pins, not the latch, because the compiler emits MOV A,P1. Input pins must be kept at 1 or the mask writes 0 back.

quiz.q: Give the direct addresses of the port SFRs P0, P1, P2 and P3, and the bit address of P1.3.
quiz.a: P0 = 80H, P1 = 90H, P2 = A0H, P3 = B0H. P1.3 is bit 3 of the register at 90H, so bit address 93H.

quiz.q: Why must software write 1 to a port bit before using that pin as an input?
quiz.a: Writing 1 switches the strong output driver off, so the pin is no longer forced low. The weak internal pull-up then holds the pin high, and an external switch or logic output can pull it low. With the latch at 0 the driver overpowers the switch and the pin always reads 0.

quiz.q: The P2 latch is 0FFH. Switches hold pins P2.0 and P2.1 at ground. The program runs MOV A,P2 / CPL P2.0. Give A and the P2 latch.
quiz.a: MOV A,P2 reads the pin: P2.0 and P2.1 are 0, others 1, so A = 1111 1100 = FCH = 252. CPL P2.0 is read-modify-write: it reads the latch FFH, complements bit 0, and writes FEH = 254 to the latch. A is unchanged at 252.

quiz.q: A program does MOV P3,#00H and then JB P3.2,KEY to test a push button to ground. Explain why the button is never seen, and give the fix.
quiz.a: MOV P3,#00H drives every P3 pin low. The strong driver holds P3.2 at 0 V, so pressing a button to ground changes nothing, and JB reads the pin, which is always 0. The jump never happens. Fix: write MOV P3,#0FFH (or SETB P3.2) before testing, so the driver is released and the pull-up holds the pin at 1.

quiz.q: List three read-pin instructions and three read-modify-write instructions for the 8051 ports, and state the rule that separates them.
quiz.a: Read-pin: MOV A,P1, MOV C,P1.0, MOV 30H,P1 (JB and JNB also read the pin). Read-modify-write: ANL P1,#0FH, CPL P1.0, DJNZ P1,rel (also INC, DEC, ORL, XRL, SETB, CLR, JBC, MOV Px.y,C). Rule: if the port is the destination of the logical or bit instruction, it is read-modify-write and uses the latch.

quiz.q: Why is P0 described as open drain, and what external component does it need for general I/O?
quiz.a: Its output stage has only a pull-down transistor, so it can pull a pin to 0 V but has no pull-up to +5 V. For general I/O add an external resistor, typically 10 kΩ, from each used pin to +5 V.

quiz.q: Name the alternate functions of P3.0 and P3.1.
quiz.a: P3.0 is RXD, the serial receive pin, and P3.1 is TXD, the serial transmit pin.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every modern microcontroller keeps the same two ideas but exposes them as configuration registers: an ARM Cortex-M GPIO port has a mode register (input, output, alternate function, analog), an output-type bit that selects push-pull or open-drain, and pull-up/pull-down controls. Because reading a whole 32-bit port register and writing it back can race with an interrupt, these chips add atomic set/reset registers (BSRR on STM32) that change single bits without a read-modify-write. Cheap port expanders such as the PCF8574 give an I²C bus eight quasi-bidirectional pins that behave much like an 8051 port, including the write-1-before-read rule. Search next for GPIO push-pull versus open-drain, bit-band aliasing, and PCF8574 keypad scanning.
